## Roadmap for today

# 1.1 Metpopulation

## Spatial Ecology Timeline


::: {.cell}

:::


## Island biogeography: MacArthur & Wilson

> Patch size and spatial configuration govern persistence through
> colonization and extinction.

![](images/islandbiog.JPG){fig-align="center"}

- **Area** → extinction rate (bigger islands, smaller extinction risk)
- **Isolation** → colonisation rate (nearer islands, higher
  colonisation)

::: notes
Groups traded off patch size against isolation with 25 cells. That is
the theory

If your individuals are allowed to disperse from a mainland source to
sourranding islands: islands closer to the mainland have a higher
colonization rate bigger islands have a smaller extinction risk.
:::

## Spreading the risk

If local extinction probability is $p_e$ and patches are
**independent**, the probability that a metapopulation of *N* patches
persists one year is:

$$1 - (p_e)^N$$


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
N <- 0:20
op <- par(mar = c(4.4, 4.6, 2.4, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 20), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "number of patches",
     ylab = "metapopulation persistence, 1 year",
     main = "each line is a local extinction probability")
cols <- hcl.colors(9, "Viridis")
for (k in 1:9) {
  pe <- k / 10
  lines(N, 1 - pe^N, lwd = 2.6, col = cols[k])
  text(20.4, 1 - pe^20, pe, cex = 0.8, col = cols[k], xpd = TRUE, adj = 0)
}
par(op)
```
:::


::: notes
This is the simplest possible argument for why metapopulations matter.

Persistence for t years in ONE patch is (1 - p_e)\^t. For N INDEPENDENT
patches in one year it is 1 - p_e\^N, which is "the probability that at
least one patch does not go extinct."

Look at the curve for p_e = 0.5. One patch gives you a coin flip. Five
patches gives you 97%. Ten gives you 99.9%. That is den Boer's (1968)
"spreading the risk," and it is why reserve networks beat single
reserves.

Now the crucial caveat, and it is: this requires INDEPENDENCE. No spatial synchrony. If
patches fluctuate together, N patches behave like far fewer, and the curve flattens dramatically. Lab B measures synchrony for exactly this
reason.
:::

## From islands to metapopulations

> Dispersal can protect a local population from extinction.

$$\frac{d \psi}{dt} = I - E$$

$$I = c \psi (1-\psi) \qquad E = \epsilon \psi$$

How to model metapopulation dynamics?

➢ each patch can be occupied (1) or unoccupied (0)

➢ at each time step, occupied patches go extinct with probability ε

➢ individuals emigrate from occupied patches with probability c

➢ objective is to estimate the fraction of patches occupied ѱ

<!-- ![](images/highcon.PNG){width = "10%"} -->

<!-- ![](images/metapop.PNG){width = "10%"} -->

::: notes
Dispersal ... . This is a schematic of our metapop. Some sites are
occupied, some aren't. At each timestep, occupied patches go extinct
with a probability...

Fraction of patches occupied over time is determined by Immigration and Extinction.

Immigration is a PRODUCT of two things: how many patches are supplying
(psi, times the per-patch emigration rate c), and how
many patches are available to receive them (1 - psi).

Extinction is simpler: only occupied patches can go extinct, so E = extinction prob multiplied by psi.

- $c$ — rate of individuals emigrating from occupied patches NOT the
  same as probability of colonization
- $epsilon$ — probability of local extinction
- $(1-psi)$ — the proportion of sites available to colonize
:::

## Metapopulation dynamic: Levins 1969
- Spatially Implicit Model: Tracks fraction of occupied patches

$$\frac{d\psi}{dt} = c \psi(1-\psi) - \epsilon \psi$$

- **Equilibrium Occupancy**:
Set $d \psi/dt = 0$ and solve:$$\psi^* = 1 - \frac{\epsilon}{c}$$

So the metapopulation persists ($\psi^* > 0$) **only when**
$c > \epsilon$.

- Limitations: Ignores spatial configuration, patch heterogeneity,  and observation error.
  
::: notes
If there are more patches in a metapop, then the extinction risk will be
lower. ...

At any point in time, what proportion of sites will go extinct?

At any point in time, what proportion of sites will be colonized?

At any point in time, what proportion of sites will be occupied?

Levins 1969 is a two-page paper in a newsletter of the Entomological
Society of America.

Note that INTERNAL colonization is permitted -- colonists come from
within the system. That contrasts with the basic island biogeography
model, where propagules arrive from an external mainland

Note what psi\* does NOT depend on: the number of patches. That is
because the Levins model treats space as implicit -- an infinite pool of
identical patches. Relaxing that is what the incidence function model
does.

c in the Levins model is the rate of individuals EMIGRATING from
occupied patches. It is NOT the same quantity as gamma, the probability
an empty patch becomes colonized in one time step, which is what a
dynamic occupancy model estimates. So "gamma \< epsilon means
extinction" does not follow from "c \< e means extinction." We will see
exactly that apparent paradox in Lab E.
:::

## Why heterogeneity matters?

Extinction rate declines with area, because:

- larger patches hold more individuals
- larger patches have more heterogeneous resources so something is always available.
- and larger patches can support metapopulation-like dynamics internally.

::: notes
There are different mechanisms for why extinction declines with area...

Moilanen & Hanski (1998) extend area to EFFECTIVE area if quality or
edge effects vary.
:::

## Why synchrony matters?

The Levins model assumed **asynchronous** patch dynamics. If that fails:

- greater vulnerability to environmental stochasticity
- higher likelihood of local and metapopulation extinction 

**Why does synchrony occur?** Localized **dispersal** · spatial
dependence in **trophic interactions** · abiotic variation such as
weather — the **Moran effect**

:::{ .notes}
This is the assumption from the spreading-the-risk slide, now examined.

The three mechanisms are worth distinguishing because they imply
different management. DISPERSAL-driven synchrony declines with distance
and could in principle be managed. The MORAN EFFECT -- shared weather --
cannot be, and it is the mechanism behind Koenig & Liebhold's (2016)
finding that North American wintering bird populations have become MORE
synchronous over 50 years of warming.

Liebhold et al. (2004) is this week's third reading and the definitive
treatment. The hard part is that these three mechanisms are very
difficult to distinguish from time series alone.

Note the INFLATIONARY EFFECT as a counterweight (Gonzalez & Holt 2002):
temporally autocorrelated environments can sometimes INCREASE population
growth through strings of good years. Autocorrelation in time is not
uniformly bad.
:::



# 1.2 Spatially Explicit Metapopulations
## Connectivity
- Incidence Function Model (Hanski 1994):
  - Patch-specific colonization depends on connectivity $S_i$ :
    $$S_i = \sum_{j \neq i} \exp(-\alpha d_{ij}) A_j$$

- **Area-Isolation Paradigm**: Patch area $A_i$ reduces extinction,
  isolation $d_{ij}$ reduces colonization.

::: notes
Levins model assumes:
- patches are **homogeneous** in area, quality, isolation
- no spatial structure — every patch is equally reachable
- patch dynamics are **asynchronous** (independent)
- c and $\epsilon$ are **constant**
- **no time lags**
- a **large number** of patches

Six assumptions, and essentially the whole subsequent literature is a
relaxation of one of them.

Homogeneity and no spatial structure -\> the incidence function model,
next. 

Hanski's patch-level connectivity metric $S$ for each patch $i$ based on
patch area $A_j$ and distance $d_{ij}$ to all other patches:

$$S_i = \sum_{j \neq i} \exp(-\alpha d_{ij}) A_j$$ \

Connectivity of any focal patch i, is a decaying function of distance
bet the focal patch and source patch alpha is the dispersal
parameter:/alpha represents average dispersal distance

sum of all other source patches j (excluding the focal patch i)


Asynchrony -\> the synchrony literature, and Lab B. Constant rates
-\> covariates on colonization and extinction, which is Lab D.

The RESCUE EFFECT is a further variant: recurrent immigration LOWERS
extinction rates, so e is not independent of f (Gotelli 1991).

Tilman & Lehman (1997) took the framework to the individual level, where
a "local population" is a site holding a single individual -- a bird
territory, a sessile organism -- with priority effects and preemption.
Same mathematics, very different biology.
Hanski (1994) relaxed the homogeneity assumptions. **Extinction depends
on patch area size and isolation.**

:::

## Take home

✓ Unoccupied sites are "rescued" by colonization from occupied sites

✓ Critical to maintain patches, even if they are currently unoccupied

✓ Connectivity of patches important for increasing colonization
probability

> More patches leads to lower metapopulation extinction risk

## Stochastic Patch Occupancy Models (SPOMs)

- **Discrete-Time First-Order Markov Chain**:
  - State transition vector for patch $i$:
    $$P(z_{i,t+1}=1) = z_{i,t}(1 - \epsilon_i) + (1 - z_{i,t}) \gamma_i(S_i)$$
- **Rescue Effect**: Recurrent immigration lowers apparent extinction
  rate

## Incidence, and a provocative shortcut

$$J_i = \frac{C_i}{C_i + E_i}$$

This means a **snapshot** of occurrence data could be used to estimate
$C_i$ and $E_i$.

**But** it assumes the metapopulation is at long-term quasi-equilibrium
— that is, persistent (Moilanen 2000).

Drop that assumption and any observed trend in occupancy is **real**,
not a stochastic wobble around equilibrium.

::: notes
This is the provocative claim in Hanski (1994): one survey, and you can
infer the dynamics. Very attractive for conservation, where time series
are rare.

And it rests entirely on the equilibrium assumption, which has real
consequences either way. Assume equilibrium and you may explain away a
genuine decline as noise. Drop it and you need time series.

Note the same equilibrium form appears in Lab E as psi\* = gamma /
(gamma + epsilon) for the dynamic occupancy model. Same algebra,
different parameters.

Applications: long-term effects of deforestation (Ferraz et al. 2007),
golden eagle occupancy dynamics (Martin et al. 2009), and Florida scrub
lizard, where Hokit et al. (2001) found the IFM and a full population
projection model gave broadly similar predicted distributions.
:::

## Example: Lepanthes rupestris Orchid

- 841 patches monitored over 10 surveys (5 years with 2 surveys per
  year)
- Surveys are grouped into 5 **Primary Periods** (years) and 2
  **Secondary Periods** (within-year surveys to account for imperfect
  detection).
- Pollock's Robust Design :
  - Population is **closed** within a year (secondary periods).
  - Population is **open** to colonization/extinction between years
    (primary periods).



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Simulate orchid robust design dataset (100 sites, 5 primary periods, 2 secondary surveys)
set.seed(42)
sites <- data.frame(siteID = 1:100,
                    x      = runif(100, 0, 1000),
                    y      = runif(100, 0, 1000), 
                    area   = runif(100, 1, 10))
# Generate presence/absence matrices (100 rows x 10 columns)
obs_matrix <- matrix(rbinom(1000, 1, 0.3), nrow = 100)
print(head(obs_matrix, 3))
```
:::


::: notes
Explain Pollock's Robust Design. 

The robust design -- primary periods open to colonization and
extinction, secondary surveys within them assumed closed -- is what
makes detection estimable (Pollock 1982). You need the repeat visits.

By surveying twice a year, we can
calculate detection probability (whether we missed the orchid when it
was actually there). This ensures our colonization and extinction
estimates are unbiased by sampling error!

:::

## Calculate Connectivity Metric


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Calculate distance matrix (in meters)
dist_matrix <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(sites$x, sites$y)))

# Define alpha (1 / mean dispersal distance of Lepanthes = 4.8 meters)
meandist <- 4.8
alpha <- 1 / meandist

# Compute S matrix algebra
g <- exp(-alpha * dist_matrix)
diag(g) <- 0
S <- rowSums(sweep(g, 2, sites$area, "*"))

cat("Connectivity S for first 5 patches:", head(S, 5), "\n")
```
:::


:::{.notes}

We use distance-weighted area. Close, massive patches contribute highly to patch i's connectivity. Alpha represents the inverse of the species' mean dispersal distance. For this orchid, seeds are wind-dispersed but drop quickly, so mean dispersal is very short (\~4.8 meters).
:::

## Projecting Metapopulation Dynamics

We can project occupancy forward over 100 years based on our estimated colonization and extinction rates.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
colext_sim <- function(occ_init, col, ext, timeframe) {
  Nsite <- length(occ_init)
  occ_out <- matrix(NA, nrow = Nsite, ncol = timeframe)
  # Step 1: Initial occupancy state
  occ_out[, 1] <- rbinom(Nsite, size = 1, prob = occ_init)
  # Step 2: Simulate transition
  for(t in 2:timeframe) {
    p_occ <- occ_out[, t-1] * (1 - ext) + (1 - occ_out[, t-1]) * col
    occ_out[, t] <- rbinom(Nsite, size = 1, prob = p_occ)
  }
  return(occ_out)
}
# Project for 20 years with colonization = 0.05, extinction = 0.15
proj <- colext_sim(occ_init = rep(0.3, 100), col = 0.05, ext = 0.15, timeframe = 20)
cat("Average fraction of patches occupied over time:\n", colMeans(proj))
```
:::


::: notes
This live projection shows how the metapopulation approaches its equilibrium occupancy over time. We can use this to run PVAs and evaluate if a species will survive long-term under different landscape configurations.
:::

## When is the metapopulation approach appropriate?

Hanski's three criteria:

1.  space is **discrete** — patchy habitat
2.  processes operate on both local population and metapopulation levels
3.  habitat is **large and permanent enough** to allow local populations
    to persist for at least a few generations

::: notes
Applications: long-term effects of deforestation (Ferraz et al. 2007),
golden eagle occupancy dynamics (Martin et al. 2009), and Florida scrub
lizard, where Hokit et al. (2001) found the IFM and a full population
projection model gave broadly similar predicted distributions.

Say this plainly: the metapopulation framework is not universal, and it
was over-applied in the 1990s. Harrison (1991) surveyed real systems and
found classic Levins-style metapopulations to be rare -- most were
mainland-island or patchy populations.

Criterion 3 is the one most often violated. If local populations blink
out within a generation, you have a patchy population, not a
metapopulation.

Our orchid meets all three: discrete moss patches on boulders and trees,
local and network dynamics, and patches persisting across years.
:::

## Source–sink dynamics

$$N_t = N_{t-1}(B + I - D - E), \qquad \lambda_t = B + I - D - E$$

|            | λ    | births vs deaths | emigration vs immigration |
|------------|------|------------------|---------------------------|
| **Source** | \> 1 | *B* \> *D*       | *E* \> *I*                |
| **Sink**   | \< 1 | *B* \< *D*       | *E* \< *I*                |

::: notes
Four vital rates: births, immigration, deaths, emigration.

Pulliam 1988 DEFINED sources and sinks using all four
rates, then in the rest of the paper focused only on births and deaths,
ignoring emigration and immigration. That shift "led to much confusion
in spatial demography" (Runge et al. 2006).

The confusion compounded when people started calling sources "net
exporters" and sinks "net importers," which emphasizes only the E and I
components -- the half Pulliam dropped.

So when you read a source-sink paper, check which definition is in use.
They are not equivalent.
:::

## Pseudo-sinks and sieves

**Pseudo-sink**: a habitat that *appears* to be a sink but is simply
**above carrying capacity**. As the local population falls back to *K*,
it stops looking like a sink.

**Sieve** (Cronin 2007): births exceed deaths, *but* emigration is so
high the population may still go locally extinct.

> Generalize to two axes: a **mobility** axis
(regional vs local dynamics) and a **compensation** axis (exporting vs
importing).

::: notes
Pseudo-sinks matter because they are an artefact of timing. Measure a
population that has just been supplemented above K and you will see
deaths exceeding births -- which looks like a sink and is not. Watkinson
& Sutherland (1995) is the original.

Sieves are the mirror-image failure of the "net exporter" framing: a
sieve is a prolific net exporter that cannot sustain itself.

The Thomas & Kunin two-axis version is the useful reframing: these are
not four discrete categories but a CONTINUUM in two dimensions. Most
real populations sit somewhere in the middle.
:::

## Source–sink dynamics implications

1.  Individuals in **sinks** are outside the species' **fundamental
    niche** 
2.  Source–sink dynamics **complicate species interactions** — a habitat
    that is a source for one species and a sink for another can look
    like asymmetric competition
3.  When sources occur, **classic metapopulation dynamics may be less
    likely** — more like **island–mainland**
4.  Central to **habitat prioritization**: practitioners may be
    unwilling to invest in sinks

::: notes
Insight 1 Pulliam (2000): dispersal limitation means suitable places go
unoccupied, AND sink dynamics mean unsuitable places are occupied. Both
break the assumption that occurrence indicates suitability, which is the
assumption every SDM makes.

Insight 2 is a nice trap to point out. Two species, one habitat,
opposite demographic outcomes, and the pattern looks like competitive
exclusion. It isn't.

Insight 4 is where it gets practically fraught. A sink can be worth
protecting if it buffers the source, or if it becomes a source under
changed conditions. Liu et al. (2011) on prioritization.
:::

## Balanced dispersal

Sites vary in **carrying capacity**, but there are **no sinks** (McPeek
& Holt 1992; Diffendorfer 1998).

Dispersal rates are **inversely related** to local carrying capacity:
high emigration from low-*K* sites, low emigration from high-*K* sites.

So the number of individuals moving between patches becomes **balanced**
— an extension of the **ideal free distribution** 

::: notes
This is the alternative to source-sink, and it explains the same
observation -- net flows between patches -- without invoking sinks at
all.

The IFD connection is exact: under the IFD, individuals distribute so
fitness is equalized, which means per-capita emigration is higher where
crowding relative to K is higher. Doncaster et al. (1997) is the
empirical support.

Worth flagging because the two models make different conservation
recommendations. Under source-sink, the low-quality patch is a drain.
Under balanced dispersal, it is simply a smaller patch pulling its
weight.
:::

# 2.1 Occupancy framework {.center}

## Imperfect Detection 

- **Raw Observations vs Latent Reality**:
  - $y_{i,j,t} = 0$ can mean **True Absence** ($z_{i,t} = 0$) OR
    **Non-Detection** ($z_{i,t} = 1, p < 1$).
  - Naive raw proportion of occupied sites ($\hat{\psi}_{\text{naive}}$)
    severely underestimates true occupancy.
- **False Negative Probability**: $(1 - p)^J$, where $J$ is the number
  of secondary visits.
- **Biological Consequence**: Masking population declines, range
  contractions, and extinction events.

::: notes
Emphasize that observed zero is ambiguous. Hierarchical models resolve
this ambiguity by explicitly estimating p.
:::

## Static Occupancy Model Structure

- **Process Sub-model**:
  $$z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_i), \quad \text{logit}(\psi_i) = \mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}$$
- **Observation Sub-model**:
  $$y_{ij} | z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_i p_{ij}), \quad \text{logit}(p_{ij}) = \mathbf{W}_{ij} \boldsymbol{\alpha}$$
- **Assumptions**:
  1.  Closure: Occupancy state $z_i$ is constant across
      $j = 1, \dots, J$ visits.
  2.  Independence of detections conditional on $z_i$.
  3.  No false positives ($P(y=1 | z=0) = 0$).

::: notes
Review static occupancy as the baseline building block before moving to
dynamic multi-season extensions.
:::

## Dynamic Occupancy Formulation (MacKenzie et al. 2003)

- **Initial State** ($t = 1$):
  $$z_{i,1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_{i,1})$$
- **State Transitions** ($t > 1$):
  $$z_{i,t} | z_{i,t-1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}\left( z_{i,t-1} \phi_{i,t-1} + (1 - z_{i,t-1}) \gamma_{i,t-1} \right)$$
- **Parameters**:
  - $\psi_1$: Initial occupancy probability
  - $\phi_{i,t-1}$: Persistence probability ($1 - \epsilon_{i,t-1}$)
  - $\gamma_{i,t-1}$: Colonization probability

::: notes
State space framing: The dynamic model parameterizes turnover through time using colonization gamma and persistence phi.

Read the Markov equation as a switch, because that is exactly what it is.

If z was 0 last year, the first term vanishes and z this year is
Bernoulli with probability gamma -- colonization. If z was 1 last year,
the second term vanishes and z this year is Bernoulli with probability
phi = 1 - epsilon -- survival, i.e. not going extinct.

One equation, two cases. That is the whole model.

The observation layer is what separates this from a SPOM. MacKenzie et
al. (2003) extended earlier colonization-extinction work (Erwin et al.
1998; Clark & Rosenzweig 1994) by handling DETECTABILITY.
:::

## Transition Probability Matrix Formulation

- State space $z_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}$:
  $$\mathbf{\Omega}_{i,t-1} = \begin{pmatrix} P(z_t=0|z_{t-1}=0) & P(z_t=1|z_{t-1}=0) \\ P(z_t=0|z_{t-1}=1) & P(z_t=1|z_{t-1}=1) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - \gamma_{i,t-1} & \gamma_{i,t-1} \\ 1 - \phi_{i,t-1} & \phi_{i,t-1} \end{pmatrix}$$
- **Equilibrium Occupancy** ($\psi^*$):
  $$\psi^* = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma + \epsilon} = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma + 1 - \phi}$$
- **State Trajectory**: Represents a first-order Markov chain.

::: notes
Show the matrix representation. Note how equilibrium occupancy matches
classic Levins metapopulation results.
:::

## Observation Process in Dynamic Occupancy

- For primary period $t$ and secondary visit
  $j \in \{1, \dots, J_{i,t}\}$:
  $$y_{ijt} | z_{it} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_{it} p_{ijt})$$

## Why this beats a SPOM

Stochastic patch occupancy models have three limitations (Moilanen
2002):

1.  they require **all sites sampled**, otherwise colonization is
    **over-estimated**
2.  they assume **area is measured correctly** — errors flatten the
    occupancy–area scaling
3.  they assume **no observation error** — false negatives cause large
    errors

Dynamic occupancy models address the third directly.

::: notes
Limitation 3 is the one dynamic occupancy models fix, and it matters
most because false negatives look exactly like extinctions. Miss a
species one year and detect it the next, and a SPOM records an
extinction followed by a colonization that never happened. Both rates
are inflated.

For our orchid, detection is high -- the book estimates p = 0.843 per
survey, and with two surveys per year the annual detection probability
is 1 - (1 - 0.843)\^2 = 0.98. So the correction is small HERE. For a
cryptic species it would be the whole ballgame.

The robust design -- primary periods open to colonization and
extinction, secondary surveys within them assumed closed -- is what
makes detection estimable (Pollock 1982). You need the repeat visits.
:::

# 3.1 Simulations
## Simulate the orchid network
![](images/orchid.jpg){width="40%"} 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1010)
n_p <- 841                        # patches

# patches scatter along a sinuous river channel, in metres
tt <- sort(runif(n_p, 0, 1))
rx <- 300 * tt + rnorm(n_p, 0, 6)
ry <- -300 * tt + 40 * sin(8 * tt) + rnorm(n_p, 0, 6)
rz <- 60 * tt + rnorm(n_p, 0, 2)          # elevation gradient along the river

area <- round(rlnorm(n_p, log(35), 1.0), 1)     # moss area, cm2
area <- pmin(area, 650)

# 3-D distance
dmat <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(rx, ry, rz)))

meandist <- 4.8             # mean seed dispersal, m (Tremblay 1997)
alpha <- 1 / meandist

plot(rx, 
     ry,
     pch = 21,
     bg = "grey85",
     cex = log(area + 1) / 3,
     xlab = "x (m)", 
     ylab = "y (m)", 
     asp = 1,
     main = "841 moss patches along the river; symbol size ~ log(area)")
c(patches = n_p,
  mean_area = round(mean(area), 1),
  max_area = max(area), 
  alpha = round(alpha, 3))
```
:::



::: notes
Lepanthes rupestris is a small wind-dispersed orchid, leaves 1.3 to 4.3
cm, flowers under 6 mm, that anchors its roots in moss patches on
boulders (epilithic) or tree trunks (epiphytic) along streams in the
Luquillo Mountains, Puerto Rico. Rocks tend to have larger populations
and higher occupancy than trees.

The sampling design is worth noting for its cleverness. 250 occupied
patches were identified first, then unoccupied patches were found by
randomly selecting three suitable moss-covered patches with no
individuals within a 5 m radius of each occupied patch. That gives you
unoccupied patches that are genuinely SUITABLE, which is what you need
to estimate colonization.

Note the THREE-DIMENSIONAL distance. The patches sit along a steep
elevation gradient, and dist() takes x, y and z without complaint. Most
connectivity work ignores the vertical dimension; along a mountain
stream that is a real omission.

Mean seed dispersal is 4.8 m, so alpha is about 0.21 -- a severely
dispersal- limited organism, which is exactly why the metapopulation
framing fits.
:::

## Simulate occupancy dynamics


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# TRUTH
b_psi   <- c(int = -2.899, area = 0.562, S = 0.185)
b_eps   <- c(int = -1.21,  area = -0.62)
logit_g <- -4.14                       # colonization, constant
p_det   <- 0.843                       # per-survey detection

n_prim <- 5; n_sec <- 2
logarea <- log(area + 1)

# connectivity S_i, ignoring occupancy 
gker <- exp(-alpha * dmat); diag(gker) <- 0
S <- as.vector(gker %*% area)
Sz <- as.numeric(scale(S))             # centres and scales S

psi1 <- plogis(b_psi["int"] + b_psi["area"] * logarea + b_psi["S"] * Sz)
eps  <- plogis(b_eps["int"] + b_eps["area"] * logarea)
gam  <- plogis(logit_g)

set.seed(1011)
z <- matrix(NA_integer_, n_p, n_prim)
z[, 1] <- rbinom(n_p, 1, psi1)
for (t in 2:n_prim) {
  pr <- z[, t - 1] * (1 - eps) + (1 - z[, t - 1]) * gam
  z[, t] <- rbinom(n_p, 1, pr)
}

# observation: two secondary surveys per primary period
y <- matrix(NA_integer_, n_p, n_prim * n_sec)
for (t in 1:n_prim) for (j in 1:n_sec) {
  y[, (t - 1) * n_sec + j] <- rbinom(n_p, 1, z[, t] * p_det)
}

# Counts as well as occupancy: holds abundance N, and
# the synchrony analysis needs a series with variance. A purely binary series
# from a patch that never changes state has sd = 0.
lamN <- exp(0.4 + 0.35 * logarea)          # expected count when occupied
N <- matrix(0L, n_p, n_prim)
for (t in 1:n_prim) N[, t] <- as.integer(z[, t] * rpois(n_p, lamN))

c(ever_occupied_true = sum(rowSums(z) > 0),
  ever_detected = sum(rowSums(y) > 0),
  detections = sum(y), non_detections = sum(y == 0),
  detection_rate = round(mean(y), 3),
  psi_star_expected = round(mean(gam / (gam + eps)), 3),
  mean_count_when_occupied = round(mean(N[z == 1]), 1))
```
:::


::: notes
Everything here is generated from the book's own estimates, so Lab D can
be scored against a known truth.

Check the printed numbers against theirs. They report 1969 detections
and 6641 non-detections, a detection rate of 0.229, 266 patches ever
occupied, and an equilibrium psi\* of 0.31. Ours should be in the same
neighbourhood.

Two things worth pointing at in the loop. The transition line

pr \<- z\[, t-1\] \* (1 - eps) + (1 - z\[, t-1\]) \* gam

IS equation 10.19 -- the switch we discussed. And note
EVER_OCCUPIED_TRUE versus EVER_DETECTED: the gap is the patches that
were occupied and never detected. With p = 0.843 and ten surveys that
gap should be tiny, which is why the book's detection correction changes
little here.

Note also colonization is CONSTANT while extinction depends on area.
That is the book's best-supported model, and it means the area-isolation
paradigm only half holds in this system -- area drives extinction,
isolation does not measurably drive colonization.
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
site_cov <- data.frame(logarea = logarea, Sz = Sz)

# a survey-level covariate: day of year, standardised
set.seed(1012)
date_mat <- matrix(scale(as.vector(
  outer(rep(1, n_p), rep(c(40, 210), n_prim)) + rnorm(n_p * n_prim * n_sec, 0, 8)
))[, 1], n_p, n_prim * n_sec)

# implicit-dynamics frame: stack primary periods as if independent
y_stack   <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:n_prim,
                     function(t) y[, (t - 1) * n_sec + 1:n_sec]))
cov_stack <- do.call(rbind, replicate(n_prim, site_cov, simplify = FALSE))
dat_stack <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:n_prim,
                     function(t) date_mat[, (t - 1) * n_sec + 1:n_sec]))

umf_occ <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = y_stack, siteCovs = cov_stack,
                             obsCovs = list(date = dat_stack))

# dynamic frame: all 10 surveys, 5 primary periods
umf_dyn <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = y, siteCovs = site_cov,
                             obsCovs = list(date = date_mat),
                             numPrimary = n_prim)
c(stacked_rows = nrow(y_stack), dynamic_sites = numSites(umf_dyn))
```
:::


::: notes
Two frames because we fit two kinds of model.

The IMPLICIT-DYNAMICS frame stacks the five primary periods on top of
each other and treats them as independent sites. That estimates AVERAGE
occupancy over time and ignores colonization and extinction entirely.
The book does this first and is explicit about the compromise: this is
repeated measures treated as independent samples, and unmarked cannot
easily fit random effects, so proceed with caution. Bayesian approaches
handle it properly (Rota et al. 2011).

The DYNAMIC frame keeps the structure: 841 sites, 10 surveys, 5 primary
periods. numPrimary is what tells unmarked where the primary boundaries
are.

On reshaping: real data arrive long, and you would reshape with
reshape2::dcast or base R. The base equivalent is one line --
xtabs(presence \~ siteID + survey_number, data = surveys) -- which is
worth knowing since reshape2 is superseded.
:::


# 3.2 Fit occupancy models
## First, ignore the dynamics


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_p_null <- occu(~ 1 ~ 1, umf_occ)
m_p_date <- occu(~ date ~ 1, umf_occ)
m_p_both <- occu(~ date + logarea ~ 1, umf_occ)

modSel(fitList(fits = list("p(.)" = m_p_null, 
                           "p(date)" = m_p_date,
                           "p(date+area)" = m_p_both)))
```
:::


::: notes
The implicit-dynamics approach: estimate AVERAGE occupancy over the five
years and ignore colonization and extinction.

The formula syntax is unmarked's and catches people out: the FIRST tilde
is the DETECTION model, the SECOND is occupancy. So `occu(~ date ~ 1)`
means detection varies with date, occupancy is constant.

We fit the detection model first, holding occupancy constant, which is
the book's sequence. Note fitList(fits = list(...)) rather than
fitList("name" = model, ...) -- both work, but the explicit form is
unambiguous.

Our simulation has CONSTANT detection, so date and area should NOT
improve the model. The book's real data strongly supported both. That
difference is honest: their detection genuinely varied, ours does not by
construction.
:::

## Now add area and isolation


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_area   <- occu(~ date + logarea ~ logarea, umf_occ)
m_S      <- occu(~ date + logarea ~ Sz, umf_occ)
m_areaS  <- occu(~ date + logarea ~ logarea + Sz, umf_occ)

modSel(fitList(fits = list("psi(.)" = m_p_both,
                           "psi(area)" = m_area,
                           "psi(S)" = m_S, 
                           "psi(area+S)" = m_areaS)))
round(coef(m_areaS), 3)
```
:::


::: notes
Now covariates on occupancy. The book's most-supported model is area +
S, with both effects positive: as patch area and connectivity increase,
occupancy increases. Their estimates are intercept -2.899, area 0.562, S
0.185, and the z-value for area is much larger, so the area effect is
stronger.

Compare our estimates to those numbers -- they are the truth we
simulated from.

One subtle point the book makes well, and it is worth repeating. When
they fitted detection alone, patch area appeared to strongly affect
DETECTABILITY. Once area was also in the occupancy model, the detection
effect shrank a lot. Their explanation: covariate effects on detection
and occupancy are not formally confounded, but the model does use shared
information during estimation. So be careful interpreting a covariate
that plausibly affects both.

Ours will show this less dramatically, because we simulated constant
detection.
:::

## Colonization and extinction, explicitly


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_dyn_null <- colext(psiformula = ~ 1,
                     gammaformula = ~ 1,
                     epsilonformula = ~ 1,
                     pformula = ~ 1, 
                     data = umf_dyn)

m_dyn_psi  <- colext(psiformula = ~ logarea + Sz,
                     gammaformula = ~ 1,
                     epsilonformula = ~ 1, 
                     pformula = ~ 1,
                     data = umf_dyn)

m_dyn_eps  <- colext(psiformula = ~ logarea + Sz,
                     gammaformula = ~ 1,
                     epsilonformula = ~ logarea, 
                     pformula = ~ 1,
                     data = umf_dyn)

m_dyn_full <- colext(psiformula = ~ logarea + Sz,
                     gammaformula = ~ Sz,
                     epsilonformula = ~ logarea,
                     pformula = ~ 1,
                     data = umf_dyn)

modSel(fitList(fits = list("null" = m_dyn_null,
                           "psi(area+S)" = m_dyn_psi,
                           "psi(area+S) eps(area)" = m_dyn_eps,
                           "+ gamma(S)"           = m_dyn_full)))
```
:::


::: notes
Four models of increasing complexity. Note colext() takes FOUR formulas:
initial occupancy, colonization (gamma), extinction (epsilon), and
detection.

The book's model ranking puts psi(area+S) with eps(area) on top, with
gamma(S) adding nothing -- delta AIC of 1.6, so within noise. Their
conclusion: patch area has a strong NEGATIVE effect on extinction, and
connectivity S is NOT a strong predictor of colonization.

That is a partial failure of the area-isolation paradigm in this system,
and it is worth dwelling on. Area does what the theory says. Isolation
does not. The book is straightforward about it rather than reaching for
an explanation.

Our simulation has constant colonization by construction, so the
gamma(S) model should also add nothing. Good -- that means the model
selection is behaving.

colext() is the slowest thing in this deck: it evaluates a two-state
hidden Markov likelihood over 841 sites and 5 periods for every optim
step.
:::

## Did it recover the truth?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
est <- coef(m_dyn_eps)

# coef() for a colext fit returns psi, then col, then ext, then det. This
# vector is in that order -- READ THE PRINTED NAMES to confirm rather than
# trusting the order, and the stopifnot catches a length mismatch.
truth_vec <- c(b_psi[["int"]], 
               b_psi[["area"]],
               b_psi[["S"]],   # psi
               logit_g,          # col
               b_eps[["int"]], 
               b_eps[["area"]],  # ext
               qlogis(p_det))     # det
stopifnot(length(est) == length(truth_vec))

data.frame(parameter  = names(est),
           estimate   = round(as.numeric(est), 3),
           truth      = round(truth_vec, 3),
           difference = round(as.numeric(est) - truth_vec, 3))

round(c(gamma = backTransform(m_dyn_eps, type = "col")@estimate,
        p     = backTransform(m_dyn_eps, type = "det")@estimate), 4)
```
:::


::: notes
Seven parameters, side by side with the values that generated the data.

Expect the psi and extinction coefficients to be close. The colonization
intercept may be noisier, because colonization events are rare -- gamma
is about 0.016, so across 841 patches and four transitions you observe
relatively few. Rare events, wide confidence intervals.

backTransform() converts from the logit scale to probabilities. Compare
gamma to 0.016 and p to 0.843.

Note the order of coef() output: initial occupancy, then colonization,
then extinction, then detection. If the truth vector and the estimate
vector were misaligned the differences would be nonsense, so read the
parameter names, do not trust the order.
:::

## Partial predictions


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ar_seq <- seq(min(logarea), max(logarea), length.out = 60)
S_seq  <- seq(min(Sz), max(Sz), length.out = 60)

nd_area <- data.frame(logarea = ar_seq, Sz = mean(Sz))
nd_S    <- data.frame(logarea = mean(logarea), Sz = S_seq)

# NOTE: predict(object, type, newdata) -- name BOTH, the 2nd positional is type
pr_psi_a <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "psi", newdata = nd_area)
pr_psi_S <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "psi", newdata = nd_S)
pr_ext_a <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "ext", newdata = nd_area)

band <- function(x, p, xlab, ylab, main, truth = NULL) {
  plot(x, p$Predicted, type = "l", lwd = 3, ylim = c(0, 1),
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = main)
  lines(x, p$lower, lty = 2); lines(x, p$upper, lty = 2)
  if (!is.null(truth)) lines(x, truth, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2.4, lty = 3)
}

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.4, 4.6, 3, 1))
band(exp(ar_seq) - 1, pr_psi_a, "patch area (cm2)", "initial occupancy",
     "psi vs area",
     plogis(b_psi["int"] + b_psi["area"] * ar_seq + b_psi["S"] * mean(Sz)))
band(S_seq, pr_psi_S, "connectivity S (scaled)", "", "psi vs S",
     plogis(b_psi["int"] + b_psi["area"] * mean(logarea) + b_psi["S"] * S_seq))
band(exp(ar_seq) - 1, pr_ext_a, "patch area (cm2)", "extinction",
     "extinction vs area",
     plogis(b_eps["int"] + b_eps["area"] * ar_seq))
par(op)
```
:::


::: notes
extinction probability falls steeply with patch area. That is the area
half of the area-isolation paradigm, and it is well supported.

The book's summary of the comparison between the implicit and dynamic
models is worth repeating: the area effect on average occupancy was
driven PARTLY by extinction dynamics, and since area also explains
occupancy at time 1, dynamics before the surveys began -- before 2000 --
presumably contributed too.

That is a nice illustration of a general point. A snapshot of occupancy
encodes the accumulated history of colonization and extinction, and you
cannot separate them without time series.
:::

# 3.3 Project forward {.center}

## Project the fitted dynamics


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nd_fit  <- data.frame(logarea = logarea, Sz = Sz)
psi_hat <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "psi", newdata = nd_fit)$Predicted
col_hat <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "col", newdata = nd_fit)$Predicted
ext_hat <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "ext", newdata = nd_fit)$Predicted

colext_sim <- function(psi0, col, ext, timeframe, reps) {
  ns <- length(psi0)
  out <- array(NA_integer_, dim = c(reps, ns, timeframe))
  out[, , 1] <- rbinom(reps * ns, 1, rep(psi0, each = reps))
  for (t in 2:timeframe) {
    prev <- out[, , t - 1]
    pr <- prev * (1 - rep(ext, each = reps)) +
          (1 - prev) * rep(col, each = reps)
    out[, , t] <- rbinom(reps * ns, 1, pr)
  }
  out
}

set.seed(1013)
proj <- colext_sim(psi_hat, col_hat, ext_hat, timeframe = 100, reps = 20)
land_mean <- apply(proj, c(1, 3), mean)          # reps x time

psi_star <- mean(col_hat / (col_hat + ext_hat))

op <- par(mar = c(4.4, 4.6, 3, 1))
matplot(t(land_mean), type = "l", lty = 1, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.25),
        ylim = c(0, 0.6), xlab = "time step",
        ylab = "proportion of patches occupied",
        main = "100-year projection, 20 realizations")
lines(colMeans(land_mean), lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = psi_star, lwd = 2.5, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
text(80, psi_star + 0.03, expression(psi^"*"), col = "firebrick", cex = 1.3)
par(op)
round(c(psi_star = psi_star, projected_end = mean(land_mean[, 100])), 3)
```
:::


::: notes
Twenty realizations of a 100-year projection, using patch-specific
colonization and extinction from the fitted model. Red dashed line is
the predicted equilibrium.

Now the apparent paradox the book raises, and it is the best teaching
moment in the chapter. Estimated extinction rates are HIGHER than
colonization rates -- gamma \< epsilon -- and yet the projection is
stable or rising. But the Levins model said persistence requires c \> e.
What gives?

Two reasons, and the second is the important one.

First, rates vary by patch, whereas Levins assumes they do not.

Second, and crucially, THE PARAMETERS ARE NOT THE SAME QUANTITY. In the
Levins model, c is the rate of individuals EMIGRATING from occupied
patches. In a dynamic occupancy model, gamma is the PROBABILITY THAT AN
EMPTY PATCH BECOMES COLONIZED in one primary period. Different units,
different meanings. Comparing them is a category error.

The right equilibrium for this model is psi\* = gamma / (gamma +
epsilon), and the projection should converge on it. Check the two
printed numbers.

Caveat the book flags: this projection ignores parameter uncertainty.
Propagating it properly needs a Bayesian treatment (Chandler et al.
2015).
:::

::: {.cell}

Connect straight back to Figure 1.3. In the implicit representation,
"distance" between (3,3) and (5,5) is a count of steps, not a
measurement. The model has no access to metres.

Ask what happens if cells are unequal in size or shape — the implicit
